Title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
Snippet: Thus far, I have argued: first, that generalizability is a central epistemological challenge in the science of LLM interpretability; and second, that progress could be made by considering particular axes of correspondence among model instances. I have also presented a case study illustrating the value of using these proposed axes to guide empirical investigation. Here, I consider possible objections to the key arguments in the paper, as well as potential replies to each objection. 

Objection: Interpretability is idiographic, not nomothetic. 

Reply: If interpretability is idiographic, then generalizability is indeed not a concern. That said, interpretability research does (arguably) appear to be nomothetic in nature, with identifying "universal" circuits as a high-level goal [Olah et al., 2020, Olah, 2023]. Further, as argued in Olah et al. [2020], (near-)universality would also make interpretability a much more tractable field: 

In the same way, the universality hypothesis determines what form of circuits research makes sense. If it was true in the strongest sense, one could imagine a kind of "periodic table of visual features" which we observe and catalogue across models. On the other hand, if it was mostly false, we would need to focus on a handful of models of particular societal importance and hope they stop changing every year. There might also be in between worlds, where some lessons transfer between models but others need to be learned from scratch. [Olah et al., 2020] Objection: Automated interpretability techniques reduce the need for generalization, as putative circuits can quickly be discovered in new model instances. 

Reply: In a world of fully automated interpretability [Conmy et al., 2023], a suite of methods would simply be applied to each model instance as necessary, perhaps reducing the need to speculate about "unobserved" instances. However, my position is that a coherent theory of generalizability would still be of value in such a world for two reasons. First, a theory of generalizability is, at root, an articulation of what makes two model instances similar or different along some dimension; it is not only useful for conducting research but could also be seen as a progress marker of research.

Title: Causal Interpretability for Machine Learning - Problems, Methods and Evaluation
Snippet: Interpretable machine learning has been widely explored and discussed in previous literature. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is no comprehensive review on causal interpretability models. For instance, Lipton [59] discusses the motivation behind creating interpretable models and categorizes interpretable models into two main categories: transparent models and post-hocs. Doshi-velez et al. [17] provide a definition of model interpretability and evaluation criteria. However, this review only proposes definitions and evaluations that are used for traditional interpretability of models and does not cover causal and counterfactual questions. Gilpin et al. [27], explain fundamental concepts of explainability and use them to classify the literature on interpretable models. Zhang and Zhu [111] review the existing interpretable models proposed for deep models used in visual domains. Du et al. [18] provide a comprehensive survey of existing interpretable methods and discuss issues that should be considered in future work. It is worth mentioning that none of the existing work discussed interpretable models from a causal perspective. In this work, we first introduce the state-of-the-art research in traditional interpretability (Sec. 2.2) and then give a detailed survey on causal interpretable models (Sec. 4). Figure 1 shows an overview of intepretable models and their classification.

Title: Towards falsifiable interpretability research
Snippet: We next review two case studies in the literature which exemplify the pitfalls of pursuing un(der)verified intuitions in deep learning, and perform a "post-mortem" to identify and explain the impediments that led to misleading conclusions (Sections 3 and 4). We then articulate a strategy to address these impediments in the form of a framework for robust, falsifiable interpretability research (Section 5). And we finish by applying our framework to strengthen an example hypothesis (Section 6). 

The motivation for this paper is not unprecedented; pleas have previously been made for greater rigor in the conduct and communication of machine learning research more broadly (Lipton and Steinhardt, 2018;Forde and Paganini, 2019), and in interpretability in particular (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017;Lipton, 2018). Both Lipton (2018) and Doshi-Velez and Kim (2017), motivated by a lack of consensus and rigor regarding the definition, aims, and practices of interpretability research, sought to clarify these factors. In the intervening time since these publications, the technical shortcomings of the approaches in our case studies have precipitated, and many of them have been amended or alternative approaches have been developed. We think it's important not just to amend theses technical shortcomings, but also to analyze them so that we can generalize across cases to identify the impediments that allowed these technical shortcomings to arise in the first place, and determine how we can conduct interpretability research in a manner that avoids these impediments. As such, the recommendations in this paper focus more specifically on interpretability practices and less on the definitions and aims that were key parts of Lipton (2018) and Doshi-Velez and Kim (2017). Our core aim is to articulate concrete ways of "doing good science" in the context of interpretability research, by way of referencing both exemplary techniques and cautionary tales.

We next review two case studies in the literature which exemplify the pitfalls of pursuing un(der)verified intuitions in deep learning, and perform a "post-mortem" to identify and explain the impediments that led to misleading conclusions (Sections 3 and 4). We then articulate a strategy to address these impediments in the form of a framework for robust, falsifiable interpretability research (Section 5). And we finish by applying our framework to strengthen an example hypothesis (Section 6). 

The motivation for this paper is not unprecedented; pleas have previously been made for greater rigor in the conduct and communication of machine learning research more broadly (Lipton and Steinhardt, 2018;Forde and Paganini, 2019), and in interpretability in particular (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017;Lipton, 2018). Both Lipton (2018) and Doshi-Velez and Kim (2017), motivated by a lack of consensus and rigor regarding the definition, aims, and practices of interpretability research, sought to clarify these factors. In the intervening time since these publications, the technical shortcomings of the approaches in our case studies have precipitated, and many of them have been amended or alternative approaches have been developed. Title: Explaining Decisions in ML Models: a Parameterized Complexity Analysis
Snippet: This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical investigation into the parameterized complexity of explanation problems in various machine learning (ML) models. Contrary to the prevalent black-box perception, our study focuses on models with transparent internal mechanisms. We address two principal types of explanation problems: abductive and contrastive, both in their local and global variants. Title: Adversarial Robustness and Explainability of Machine Learning Models
Snippet: Machine learning (ML) models, particularly neural networks, have gained widespread adoption owing to their exceptional performance in various domains. However, their increasing prevalence has brought forth concerns regarding their robustness and interpretability. Existing research highlights the pressing need for comprehensive methodologies and tools to address these challenges. 

Kumar et al. [14] identified a significant gap in industry practitioners' capabilities to defend their systems against adversarial attacks and manipulation. They observed a lack of essential tools among many organizations, indicating a clear demand for guidance in this area. These findings are supported by seminal research studies [21,22], underscoring the urgency of enhancing model robustness and interpretability. 

The empirical evidence and theoretical insights provided by these studies underscore the necessity for the development of comprehensive methodologies and frameworks. Such measures are essential for addressing vulnerabilities and enhancing the explainability of ML models. Rigorous investigations conducted by these studies emphasize the critical importance of exploring robustness evaluation techniques and interpretability frameworks within the context of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. 

Interpreting and explaining model predictions are crucial for establishing trust and promoting fairness and transparency in AI/ML systems [6,7,23]. This trust can be weakened through the use of Adversarial attacks [3]. These attacks generate model inputs that include noise that is imperceptible to human recognition but leads the model to classify the input incorrectly. By understanding the factors contributing to model decisions, stakeholders can have confidence in the system's reliability and accountability [2]. Interpretation methods also facilitate the detection and mitigation of biases, ensuring equitable treatment across demographics and minimizing discriminatory outcomes. 

Explanations generated from interpretation methods not only empower end-users to understand the reasoning behind AI-generated predictions but also facilitate regulatory compliance and ethical decision-making processes. Advancements in interpretability research significantly contribute to the responsible development and deployment of AI technologies, bolstering public trust and fostering the adoption of AI systems in critical domains. 

We introduce the "Adversarial Observation" framework, a Pythonbased toolkit designed to facilitate the implementation of adversarial attacks and Explainable AI (XAI) techniques during machine learning model training.

Title: Methods for interpreting and understanding deep neural networks
Snippet: Building transparent machine learning systems is a convergent approach to both extracting novel domain knowledge and performing model validation. As machine learning is increasingly used in real-world decision processes, the necessity for transparent machine learning will continue to grow. Examples that illustrate the limitations of black-box methods were mentioned in Section 8.1. 

This tutorial has covered two key directions for improving machine learning transparency: interpreting the concepts learned by a model by building prototypes, and explaining of the model's decisions by identifying the relevant input variables. The discussion mainly abstracted from the exact choice of deep neural network, training procedure, or application domain. Instead, we have focused on the more conceptual developments, and connected them to recent practical successes reported in the literature. 

In particular we have discussed the effect of linking prototypes to the data, via a data density function or a generative model. We have described the crucial difference between sensitivity analysis and decomposition in terms of what these analyses seek to explain. Finally, we have outlined the benefit in terms of robustness, of treating the explanation problem with graph propagation techniques rather than with standard analysis techniques. 

This tutorial has focused on post-hoc interpretability, where we do not have full control over the model's structure. Instead, the techniques of interpretation should apply to a general class of nonlinear machine learning models, no matter how they were trained and who trained themeven fully trained models that are available for download like BVLC CaffeNet [24] or GoogleNet [50] In that sense the presented novel technological development in ML allowing for interpretability is an orthogonal strand of research independent of new developments for improving neural network models and their learning algorithms. This trust can be weakened through the use of Adversarial attacks [3]. These attacks generate model inputs that include noise that is imperceptible to human recognition but leads the model to classify the input incorrectly. By understanding the factors contributing to model decisions, stakeholders can have confidence in the system's reliability and accountability [2]. Interpretation methods also facilitate the detection and mitigation of biases, ensuring equitable treatment across demographics and minimizing discriminatory outcomes. 

Explanations generated from interpretation methods not only empower end-users to understand the reasoning behind AI-generated predictions but also facilitate regulatory compliance and ethical decision-making processes. Advancements in interpretability research significantly contribute to the responsible development and deployment of AI technologies, bolstering public trust and fostering the adoption of AI systems in critical domains. 

We introduce the "Adversarial Observation" framework, a Pythonbased toolkit designed to facilitate the implementation of adversarial attacks and Explainable AI (XAI) techniques during machine learning model training.

[5] provide a comprehensive survey of Explainable AI (XAI) methods, highlighting the importance of transparency for building trust in AI systems. Molnar [54] offers practical guidance for making machine learning models interpretable, with specific techniques applicable to sensor calibration applications. 

For industrial deployment, interpretability serves multiple purposes: validating that learned models align with physical understanding, diagnosing prediction errors, satisfying regulatory requirements, and building operator trust. These considerations motivate the incorporation of SHAP analysis in the proposed PI-ADC framework.

Building transparent machine learning systems is a convergent approach to both extracting novel domain knowledge and performing model validation. As machine learning is increasingly used in real-world decision processes, the necessity for transparent machine learning will continue to grow. Examples that illustrate the limitations of black-box methods were mentioned in Section 8.1. 

This tutorial has covered two key directions for improving machine learning transparency: interpreting the concepts learned by a model by building prototypes, and explaining of the model's decisions by identifying the relevant input variables. The discussion mainly abstracted from the exact choice of deep neural network, training procedure, or application domain. Instead, we have focused on the more conceptual developments, and connected them to recent practical successes reported in the literature. 

In particular we have discussed the effect of linking prototypes to the data, via a data density function or a generative model. We have described the crucial difference between sensitivity analysis and decomposition in terms of what these analyses seek to explain. Finally, we have outlined the benefit in terms of robustness, of treating the explanation problem with graph propagation techniques rather than with standard analysis techniques. 

This tutorial has focused on post-hoc interpretability, where we do not have full control over the model's structure. Instead, the techniques of interpretation should apply to a general class of nonlinear machine learning models, no matter how they were trained and who trained themeven fully trained models that are available for download like BVLC CaffeNet [24] or GoogleNet [50] In that sense the presented novel technological development in ML allowing for interpretability is an orthogonal strand of research independent of new developments for improving neural network models and their learning algorithms. We would like to stress that all new developments can in this sense always profit in addition from interpretability.

Below is a synthesis of the interpretability literature on whether existing methods provide “comprehensive” understanding of model decision-making, and how the term “comprehensive” is often conflationed.

Summary answer
- The literature does not support a single, strong conclusion that “no method” ever yields comprehensive understanding; rather, it supports multiple, context-dependent limits and trade-offs. <cite id="d810dc83-1">There is no consensus definition of interpretability</cite>, and <cite id="df066c4f-2">explanations are “models of the model” that must balance understandability with fidelity</cite>. Consequently, claims that “no existing method” is comprehensive typically collapse distinct notions—global mechanistic coverage, causal faithfulness, task-specific robustness, and human usability—into a single bar for “comprehensiveness.” <cite id="df066c4f-1">Absent a cohesive definition, it is difficult to assess the quality of interpretability techniques</cite>.

What “comprehensive” means (and why it diverges across subfields)
- Distinguish interpretability (intrinsic transparency of the system) from explainability (post hoc explanations tailored to humans). <cite id="df066c4f-2">Interpretability treats models whose logic can be traced by inspection (e.g., small decision trees) as transparent; explainability covers methods like feature importance, visualization, and nearest neighbors that provide human-understandable approximations of model behavior</cite>. <cite id="df066c4f-2">An explanation is an interface that must be both accurate in the regions of interest and understandable to humans</cite>. <cite id="d810dc83-1">Practitioners emphasize that lack of a unified definition and metrics hinders assessing interpretability quality</cite>.
- Recent surveys echo that “comprehensiveness” is not a universal property but a design goal shaped by domain and use. <cite id="d810dc83-3">Even in cutting-edge architectures like Mixture-of-Experts, current interpretability analyses rely on specific metrics and qualitative examples, with comprehensive standardized metrics for expert specialization identified as open research</cite>. <cite id="d810dc83-4">Both academia and industry lack a unified definition of interpretability, motivating scoped definitions aligned to application needs</cite>.

Evidence that existing methods do not yet deliver comprehensive understanding
- LLM introspection and self-explanation: <cite id="84056bda-0">Self-reflection can reduce hallucinations and support agentic behaviors, but subsequent studies show it is not universally reliable and may degrade performance under some conditions</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-1">Faithful introspection is a prerequisite for using verbalized rationales as oversight, yet the authors argue introspection remains complementary to more rigorous internal tools (probes, sparse autoencoders, circuit discovery) and its faithfulness may fail when models learn to be unaligned or dishonest</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-2">Audits of reasoning chains show RLLMs can iteratively reinforce biases and errors; interventions at the origin of hallucinations often fail to reverse effects due to “chain disloyalty,” and existing detection methods lose reliability in complex chains</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-3">Surveys of hallucination reveal multiple modes (factual, faithfulness, logical) and training-phase dependencies, underscoring that high-level model “confidence” does not equal correct internal reasoning</cite>.
- Attribution/robustness and feature-level analysis: <cite id="84056bda-4">Output-level and probabilistic uncertainty methods can fail when models express high confidence in incorrect content; self-consistency cannot distinguish consistently erroneous information; evidence retrieval faces scalability limits</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-4">Layer-level internal analyses highlight distributional differences between hallucinatory and factual content, but they often overlook internal feature importance, leaving open questions about efficient focus on discriminative subsets</cite>. Together, these findings show that popular explanation methods frequently misattribute causes, lack robustness across conditions, or fail to reach the local/global grain needed for trustworthy oversight.
- Mechanistic interpretability (MI) shows progress but explicit gaps: <cite id="3501e8c4-3">MI reverse-engineers transformer computations into human-understandable mechanisms (neurons, attention heads, circuits), promising insights and safety benefits, yet concerns remain about scalability and generalizability to address core AI safety problems</cite>. <cite id="3501e8c4-4">Polysemanticity—neurons participating in multiple unrelated behaviors—challenges causal attribution; sparse autoencoders improve interpretability by decomposing activations into features, but mapping these features into stable behavioral policies remains an active challenge</cite>. <cite id="3501e8c4-2">MI has been used to link properties like toxicity, linguistic features, and tasks to identifiable components (neurons, MHSA, FFN, layers, circuits), yet coverage across all behaviors and robust identification at scale remains limited</cite>.
- Architectural specialization and specialization-specific limits: <cite id="d810dc83-3">In MoE models, current interpretability analyses are indicative and metrics are not standardized; understanding expert specialization comprehensively remains an open area</cite>. This illustrates that even as architectures scale, the interpretability tooling does not uniformly scale to explain why each component behaves as it does across inputs and tasks.

How “comprehensive” is often conflated
- Goal confusion: <cite id="df066c4f-2">Explanations approximate behavior in a comprehensible way, but the “model of the model” must be accurate where it matters; outside those regions, comprehensiveness is over-claimed</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-1">Treating introscribed rationales as evidence of true decision-making presumes causal coupling; absent verification, these explanations are not comprehensive understandings of the decision process</cite>.
- Scope: <cite id="3501e8c4-3">In MI, “mechanistic” explanations cover internal components and circuits, yet surveys stress scalability and generalizability limits, so coverage is not global across all behaviors or models</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-2">Audits show that even targeted interventions can fail to correct later-chain errors, showing that local explanations do not guarantee globally consistent or correct behavior</cite>.
- Definitions: <cite id="d810dc83-1">Practical domains list multiple definitions (human-understandable explanations; understanding causes; users correctly and efficiently predicting results), which differ in strength and scope</cite>. Confusing these definitions turns a failure to meet one (e.g., robust causal faithfulness) into an alleged failure to achieve “comprehensiveness” in a stronger, design-specific sense.

What the literature does support (and where progress is plausible)
- Progress is measurable along multiple axes, not a single binary threshold. <cite id="d810dc83-3">Standardized metrics for specialized components (e.g., MoE experts) are missing and actively researched</cite>, and <cite id="3501e8c4-4">advances like sparse autoencoders and circuit-level analyses extend coverage from neurons to more stable features and circuits</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-0">Causal analyses and white-box techniques can explain self-reflection mechanisms, but typically at local or latent levels with limited generalization</cite>.
- Robustness conditions matter. <cite id="84056bda-1">Faithfulness of introspection requires verified causal coupling before explanations can be treated as evidence of decision-making</cite>, and <cite id="84056bda-2">even interventions can fail due to chain disloyalty in reasoning trajectories</cite>. These indicate that “comprehensiveness” requires guarantees (robustness) and cross-arcana consistency (across explanations, data, and time), which current methods do not uniformly provide.

Practical implications
- Do not equate “useful explanation” with “comprehensive mechanism.” <cite id="df066c4f-2">Choose intrinsic or post hoc methods matching the required grain (global patterns vs. per-instance causes) and verify that the “model of the model” is accurate in the region of interest</cite>. <cite id="d810dc83-1">In regulated settings, adopt scoped definitions tied to user goals and risk, with evaluation metrics aligned to those goals</cite>.
- Demand robustness claims. <cite id="84056bda-1">Audit causal coupling for introspective rationales</cite> and <cite id="84056bda-2">test whether interventions propagate and generalize across chains</cite>. <cite id="3501e8c4-3">For MI, assess scalability and generalizability for the safety/alignment problem at hand</cite>.
- Expect partial-to-moderate coverage. <cite id="3501e8c4-4">Polysemantic activation spaces limit neuron-level causal claims; feature-based and circuit-based analyses expand coverage but still leave gaps</cite>. <cite id="d810dc83-3">In MoE systems, specialization interpretability remains an open problem</cite>. Together, these support a cautious conclusion: there are strong, documented limits; “comprehensive” in a universal sense is not yet a safe assumption.

Bottom line
- The interpretability literature supports nuanced, conditional limits: methods can deliver locally faithful, task-tailored, and increasingly mechanistic understandings, but they do not uniformly achieve globally faithful, robustly generalizable, and causally complete accounts of decision-making across all domains and behaviors. <cite id="df066c4f-1">The lack of a cohesive definition and metrics</cite>, <cite id="84056bda-0">unreliable or prompt-sensitive introspection</cite>, <cite id="84056bda-2">chain disloyalty and intervention failure in reasoning</cite>, <cite id="84056bda-4">failure of common attribution/uncertainty heuristics</cite>, and <cite id="3501e8c4-3">MI’s scalability and generalizability concerns</cite> all illustrate why strong “no-method” claims are unsupported, while careful, scoped claims about incompleteness are well supported. <cite id="d810dc83-1">Most disagreements about “comprehensiveness” trace to conflating different definitions and goals—human-understandable explanation, causal understanding, robust auditing, and usability—rather than a single technical failure mode</cite>.

Title: ReBeCA: Unveiling Interpretable Behavior Hierarchy behind the Iterative Self-Reflection of Language Models with Causal Analysis
Snippet: Inspired by self-reflection as a cognitive strategy for consolidating human experience, prior work has incorporated self-reflection into language models as a mechanism for reducing hallucinations and enabling agentic behaviors (Madaan et al., 2023;Shinn et al., 2023). However, subsequent empirical studies have shown that self-reflection is not universally reliable and may even degrade performance under certain conditions (Huang et al., 2023). 

In response, recent work has begun to examine the behaviors that models exhibit during selfreflection, showing that certain semantic cues and revision patterns recur across reflection rounds and are correlated with the self-reflection out-come (Kamoi et al., 2024;Yan et al., 2025). Other studies investigate factors such as over-confidence, prompt sensitivity, or refinement depth, linking them to self-reflection effectiveness (Xu et al., 2024;Kirchhof et al., 2025;Huang et al., 2023). Although these analyzes provide useful empirical observations, they often focus on individual factors or isolated steps without modeling how behaviors evolve and interact across multiple rounds. 

Several recent works attempt to address these limitations by examining self-reflection from a temporal or mechanistic perspective. Some modify the design or constraints of self-reflection procedures to probe whether language models genuinely exhibit self-correction capabilities (Li et al., 2024), while others adopt white-box analytical approaches, inspecting internal activations or parameter-level behaviors to explain self-reflection (Stechly et al., 2024). While informative, these approaches typically emphasize local mechanisms or latent features, which are difficult to interpret at the behavioral level and may not generalize across tasks or model settings. Overall, prior research provides valuable insights into self-reflection but largely lacks trajectory-level analyses that model selfreflection as a structured, multi-round process.
</snippet>

Title: Introspective Coupling: Self-Explanation Training Tracks Behavioral Change Despite Fixed Supervision
Snippet: Faithful introspection is a prerequisite for using model explanations as a tool for oversight of language models: if a model's verbalized rationales causally track its behavior, downstream users and auditors can use those rationales to anticipate, debug, and contest model decisions, including in safety-critical domains such as misalignment detection. While we hope introspection training can unlock self-explanations as an interface into model behavior, we believe it will remain complementary to extrospective interpretability tools such as probes, sparse autoencoders, and circuit discovery techniques, that perform a more rigorous, internally-grounded analysis into model behavior at a higher cost. Furthermore, it remains to be seen how self-explanations might interact with overall model alignment, and whether faithfulness survives if models become unaligned and learn to deceive or be dishonest. Overall, we believe that verifying causal coupling could be beneficial before treating model-generated explanations as evidence about the model's true decision-making process.
</snippet>

Title: Auditing Meta-Cognitive Hallucinations in Reasoning Large Language Models
Snippet: The development of Reasoning Large Language Models (RLLMs) has significantly improved multi-step reasoning capabilities, but it has also made hallucination problems more frequent and harder to eliminate. While existing approaches mitigate hallucinations through external knowledge integration, model parameter analysis, or self-verification, they often fail to capture how hallucinations emerge and evolve across the reasoning chain. In this work, we study the causality of hallucinations under constrained knowledge domains by auditing the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectory and assessing the model's cognitive confidence in potentially erroneous or biased claims. Our analysis reveals that in long-CoT settings, RLLMs can iteratively reinforce biases and errors through flawed reflective reasoning, eventually leading to hallucinated reasoning paths. Surprisingly, even direct interventions at the origin of hallucinations often fail to reverse their effects, as reasoning chains exhibit'chain disloyalty'-- a resistance to correction and a tendency to preserve flawed logic. Furthermore, we show that existing hallucination detection methods are less reliable and interpretable than previously assumed in complex reasoning scenarios. Unlike methods such as circuit tracing that require access to model internals, our black-box auditing approach supports interpretable long-chain hallucination attribution, offering better generalizability and practical utility. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Winnie-Lian/AHa_Meta_Cognitive
</snippet>

Title: A Novel Differential Feature Learning for Effective Hallucination Detection and Classification
Snippet: Large language models frequently generate hallucinations that pose significant challenges for real-world deployment. In healthcare applications, hallucinated medical information could impact patient care decisions, while in legal contexts, factually incorrect analysis could affect case outcomes. Financial systems face risks from erroneous market analysis leading to poor investment decisions. These high-stakes applications have driven extensive research into hallucination detection methods, with approaches evolving from simple confidencebased measures to sophisticated internal representation analysis. 

Early detection efforts focused on output-level validation methods. Uncertainty estimation approaches measure model confidence through entropy and predictive variance [5], [6], while masked language model techniques analyze probability distributions to identify inconsistencies [7]. Self-consistency methods generate multiple responses to the same query and identify variations as potential hallucinations [8]. Contrastive learning approaches train models to distinguish between factual and hallucinated content through explicit negative sampling [10]. Evidence retrieval methods decompose generated text into atomic facts and verify them against external knowledge sources [15], while cross-model validation employs one  language model to audit another's outputs through systematic examination [16]. However, these approaches face inherent limitations: uncertainty methods fail when models express high confidence in incorrect content [7], self-consistency cannot distinguish consistently erroneous information [8], and evidence retrieval encounters scalability challenges [15], [16]. 

Motivated by these limitations, recent research has shifted toward internal representation analysis as an alternative paradigm. Studies have shown that specific hidden layers exhibit distributional differences between hallucinatory and factual content [11]. Building upon the Transformer architecture [17], differential attention mechanisms have demonstrated efficacy in amplifying task-relevant information while attenuating noise [13]. However, current layer-level approaches process entire hidden representations uniformly, typically extracting complete 768-dimensional vectors without examining internal feature importance. 

While layer-level analysis has advanced understanding of hallucination mechanisms, it overlooks the internal structure of hidden representations. Few studies have systematically examined which specific feature dimensions within layers carry hallucination-relevant information. This leaves open questions about whether detection systems could operate more efficiently by focusing on discriminative feature subsets rather than processing entire representations.

Snippet: Mechanistic interpretability and sparse features. Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer neural networks into humanunderstandable components and algorithms (Olsson et al., 2022). Early successes in Transformers include the identification of induction heads as a core mechanism supporting in-context learning (Olsson et al., 2022). More broadly, the field has developed a toolkit for locating and causally validating candidate mechanisms, including activation patching, causal ablation, and direction-based interventions. A central challenge in this literature is polysemanticity, where individual neurons participate in multiple unrelated behaviors. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) address this by decomposing activations into more interpretable features, often providing a more useful basis for mechanistic analysis than raw neurons alone (Cunningham et al., 2023). Our work builds on this paradigm by using SAE features as the interpretable basis of a symbolic behavioral policy. 

Symbolic models of neural behavior. A growing line of work seeks to distill neural computations into explicit symbolic representations. Recent work on circuit distillation extracts human-readable algorithmic descriptions from mechanistically identified circuits (Wadhwa et al., 2025). Closely related, symbolic-mechanistic evaluation combines symbolic behavioral descriptions with mechanistic interventions to test whether a model is not only accurate, but internally consistent with an intended mechanism (Habibi et al., 2026). Our work is aligned with this tradition, but uses a symbolic model for a different purpose: not only to describe behavior, but to serve as the target of training-data attribution. In SMDA, the symbolic object is a learned policy over SAE features, which allows attribution to operate over an interpretable behavioral representation even when no single circuit is known in advance. 

Training-data attribution and influence functions. Influence functions estimate how upweighting or removing a training example changes model parameters or predictions (Koh and Liang, 2017). Subsequent work has adapted these ideas to modern language models, including scalable approximations for studying generalization behavior in LLMs (Grosse et al., 2023).

Below is a synthesis of the interpretability literature on whether existing methods provide “comprehensive” understanding of model decision-making, and how the term “comprehensive” is often conflationed.

Summary answer
- The literature does not support a single, strong conclusion that “no method” ever yields comprehensive understanding; rather, it supports multiple, context-dependent limits and trade-offs. <cite id="d810dc83-1">There is no consensus definition of interpretability</cite>, and <cite id="df066c4f-2">explanations are “models of the model” that must balance understandability with fidelity</cite>. Consequently, claims that “no existing method” is comprehensive typically collapse distinct notions—global mechanistic coverage, causal faithfulness, task-specific robustness, and human usability—into a single bar for “comprehensiveness.” <cite id="df066c4f-1">Absent a cohesive definition, it is difficult to assess the quality of interpretability techniques</cite>.

What “comprehensive” means (and why it diverges across subfields)
- Distinguish interpretability (intrinsic transparency of the system) from explainability (post hoc explanations tailored to humans). <cite id="df066c4f-2">Interpretability treats models whose logic can be traced by inspection (e.g., small decision trees) as transparent; explainability covers methods like feature importance, visualization, and nearest neighbors that provide human-understandable approximations of model behavior</cite>. <cite id="df066c4f-2">An explanation is an interface that must be both accurate in the regions of interest and understandable to humans</cite>. <cite id="d810dc83-1">Practitioners emphasize that lack of a unified definition and metrics hinders assessing interpretability quality</cite>.
- Recent surveys echo that “comprehensiveness” is not a universal property but a design goal shaped by domain and use. <cite id="d810dc83-3">Even in cutting-edge architectures like Mixture-of-Experts, current interpretability analyses rely on specific metrics and qualitative examples, with comprehensive standardized metrics for expert specialization identified as open research</cite>. <cite id="d810dc83-4">Both academia and industry lack a unified definition of interpretability, motivating scoped definitions aligned to application needs</cite>.

- Attribution/robustness and feature-level analysis: <cite id="84056bda-4">Output-level and probabilistic uncertainty methods can fail when models express high confidence in incorrect content; self-consistency cannot distinguish consistently erroneous information; evidence retrieval faces scalability limits</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-4">Layer-level internal analyses highlight distributional differences between hallucinatory and factual content, but they often overlook internal feature importance, leaving open questions about efficient focus on discriminative subsets</cite>. Together, these findings show that popular explanation methods frequently misattribute causes, lack robustness across conditions, or fail to reach the local/global grain needed for trustworthy oversight.
- Mechanistic interpretability (MI) shows progress but explicit gaps: <cite id="3501e8c4-3">MI reverse-engineers transformer computations into human-understandable mechanisms (neurons, attention heads, circuits), promising insights and safety benefits, yet concerns remain about scalability and generalizability to address core AI safety problems</cite>. <cite id="3501e8c4-4">Polysemanticity—neurons participating in multiple unrelated behaviors—challenges causal attribution; sparse autoencoders improve interpretability by decomposing activations into features, but mapping these features into stable behavioral policies remains an active challenge</cite>. <cite id="3501e8c4-2">MI has been used to link properties like toxicity, linguistic features, and tasks to identifiable components (neurons, MHSA, FFN, layers, circuits), yet coverage across all behaviors and robust identification at scale remains limited</cite>.
- Architectural specialization and specialization-specific limits: <cite id="d810dc83-3">In MoE models, current interpretability analyses are indicative and metrics are not standardized; understanding expert specialization comprehensively remains an open area</cite>. This illustrates that even as architectures scale, the interpretability tooling does not uniformly scale to explain why each component behaves as it does across inputs and tasks.

How “comprehensive” is often conflated
- Goal confusion: <cite id="df066c4f-2">Explanations approximate behavior in a comprehensible way, but the “model of the model” must be accurate where it matters; outside those regions, comprehensiveness is over-claimed</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-1">Treating introscribed rationales as evidence of true decision-making presumes causal coupling; absent verification, these explanations are not comprehensive understandings of the decision process</cite>.
- Scope: <cite id="3501e8c4-3">In MI, “mechanistic” explanations cover internal components and circuits, yet surveys stress scalability and generalizability limits, so coverage is not global across all behaviors or models</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-2">Audits show that even targeted interventions can fail to correct later-chain errors, showing that local explanations do not guarantee globally consistent or correct behavior</cite>.
- Definitions: <cite id="d810dc83-1">Practical domains list multiple definitions (human-understandable explanations; understanding causes; users correctly and efficiently predicting results), which differ in strength and scope</cite>. Confusing these definitions turns a failure to meet one (e.g., robust causal faithfulness) into an alleged failure to achieve “comprehensiveness” in a stronger, design-specific sense.

What the literature does support (and where progress is plausible)
- Progress is measurable along multiple axes, not a single binary threshold. <cite id="d810dc83-3">Standardized metrics for specialized components (e.g., MoE experts) are missing and actively researched</cite>, and <cite id="3501e8c4-4">advances like sparse autoencoders and circuit-level analyses extend coverage from neurons to more stable features and circuits</cite>. <cite id="84056bda-0">Causal analyses and white-box techniques can explain self-reflection mechanisms, but typically at local or latent levels with limited generalization</cite>.
- Robustness conditions matter. <cite id="84056bda-1">Faithfulness of introspection requires verified causal coupling before explanations can be treated as evidence of decision-making</cite>, and <cite id="84056bda-2">even interventions can fail due to chain disloyalty in reasoning trajectories</cite>. These indicate that “comprehensiveness” requires guarantees (robustness) and cross-arcana consistency (across explanations, data, and time), which current methods do not uniformly provide.

Practical implications
- Do not equate “useful explanation” with “comprehensive mechanism.” <cite id="df066c4f-2">Choose intrinsic or post hoc methods matching the required grain (global patterns vs. per-instance causes) and verify that the “model of the model” is accurate in the region of interest</cite>. <cite id="d810dc83-1">In regulated settings, adopt scoped definitions tied to user goals and risk, with evaluation metrics aligned to those goals</cite>.
- Demand robustness claims. <cite id="84056bda-1">Audit causal coupling for introspective rationales</cite> and <cite id="84056bda-2">test whether interventions propagate and generalize across chains</cite>. <cite id="3501e8c4-3">For MI, assess scalability and generalizability for the safety/alignment problem at hand</cite>.
- Expect partial-to-moderate coverage. <cite id="3501e8c4-4">Polysemantic activation spaces limit neuron-level causal claims; feature-based and circuit-based analyses expand coverage but still leave gaps</cite>. <cite id="d810dc83-3">In MoE systems, specialization interpretability remains an open problem</cite>. Bottom line
- The interpretability literature supports nuanced, conditional limits: methods can deliver locally faithful, task-tailored, and increasingly mechanistic understandings, but they do not uniformly achieve globally faithful, robustly generalizable, and causally complete accounts of decision-making across all domains and behaviors. <cite id="df066c4f-1">The lack of a cohesive definition and metrics</cite>, <cite id="84056bda-0">unreliable or prompt-sensitive introspection</cite>, <cite id="84056bda-2">chain disloyalty and intervention failure in reasoning</cite>, <cite id="84056bda-4">failure of common attribution/uncertainty heuristics</cite>, and <cite id="3501e8c4-3">MI’s scalability and generalizability concerns</cite> all illustrate why strong “no-method” claims are unsupported, while careful, scoped claims about incompleteness are well supported. <cite id="d810dc83-1">Most disagreements about “comprehensiveness” trace to conflating different definitions and goals—human-understandable explanation, causal understanding, robust auditing, and usability—rather than a single technical failure mode</cite>.

Title: Evolutionary approaches to explainable machine learning
Snippet: The terms interpretability and explainability are often used interchangeably by researchers. However, in this chapter we distinguish between them as referring to two different but related aspects of attempting to understand a model [30,41]. 

For our purposes, interpretability refers to the level of transparency and ease of understanding of a model's decision-making process. An interpretable model is one whose decisions can be traced and understood by a human, for example, by having a simple symbolic representation. In other words, a model is considered interpretable if its decision-making process can be understood simply by inspecting the model. For example, small decision trees are often considered interpretable because it is feasible for a human to follow the exact steps leading to the prediction. 

On the other hand, even if we cannot trace the exact logic, a model can still be considered explainable if a human-understandable explanation can be provided for what the model is doing or why a decision is made. The more comprehensive and understandable the explanation is, the more explainable the overall system is. Explanations can be provided for the overall patterns and relationships learned by a model, or for the logic used to produce an individual prediction. Some practical methods for providing explanations include evaluating feature importance, visualizing intermediate representations, or comparing the prediction to be explained with samples from the training set. An explanation essentially acts as an interface between the human and the model, attempting to approximate the behavior or decisions made by the model in a way that is comprehensible to humans. As such, this "model of the model" must be both an accurate proxy for the model in the areas of interest but also be understandable itself. 

These two terms, interpretability and explainability, also roughly correspond to two paradigms for improving the understandability of a model. The first approach, often known as "intrinsic interpretability", "glass-box" or "interpretability by design", focuses on the interpretability of the model and aims to improve it by simplifying or otherwise restricting its complexity [34]. A simple enough model allows the exact logic to be easily followed and understood by humans, but over-reducing the model complexity can also restrict the performance of the model. In some cases, it might not be possible to construct a simple enough model that can still effectively solve the problem at hand.

Title: ReBeCA: Unveiling Interpretable Behavior Hierarchy behind the Iterative Self-Reflection of Language Models with Causal Analysis
Snippet: Inspired by self-reflection as a cognitive strategy for consolidating human experience, prior work has incorporated self-reflection into language models as a mechanism for reducing hallucinations and enabling agentic behaviors (Madaan et al., 2023;Shinn et al., 2023). However, subsequent empirical studies have shown that self-reflection is not universally reliable and may even degrade performance under certain conditions (Huang et al., 2023). 

In response, recent work has begun to examine the behaviors that models exhibit during selfreflection, showing that certain semantic cues and revision patterns recur across reflection rounds and are correlated with the self-reflection out-come (Kamoi et al., 2024;Yan et al., 2025). Other studies investigate factors such as over-confidence, prompt sensitivity, or refinement depth, linking them to self-reflection effectiveness (Xu et al., 2024;Kirchhof et al., 2025;Huang et al., 2023). Although these analyzes provide useful empirical observations, they often focus on individual factors or isolated steps without modeling how behaviors evolve and interact across multiple rounds. 

Several recent works attempt to address these limitations by examining self-reflection from a temporal or mechanistic perspective. Some modify the design or constraints of self-reflection procedures to probe whether language models genuinely exhibit self-correction capabilities (Li et al., 2024), while others adopt white-box analytical approaches, inspecting internal activations or parameter-level behaviors to explain self-reflection (Stechly et al., 2024). While informative, these approaches typically emphasize local mechanisms or latent features, which are difficult to interpret at the behavioral level and may not generalize across tasks or model settings. Overall, prior research provides valuable insights into self-reflection but largely lacks trajectory-level analyses that model selfreflection as a structured, multi-round process.

Title: Introspective Coupling: Self-Explanation Training Tracks Behavioral Change Despite Fixed Supervision
Snippet: Faithful introspection is a prerequisite for using model explanations as a tool for oversight of language models: if a model's verbalized rationales causally track its behavior, downstream users and auditors can use those rationales to anticipate, debug, and contest model decisions, including in safety-critical domains such as misalignment detection. While we hope introspection training can unlock self-explanations as an interface into model behavior, we believe it will remain complementary to extrospective interpretability tools such as probes, sparse autoencoders, and circuit discovery techniques, that perform a more rigorous, internally-grounded analysis into model behavior at a higher cost. Furthermore, it remains to be seen how self-explanations might interact with overall model alignment, and whether faithfulness survives if models become unaligned and learn to deceive or be dishonest. Overall, we believe that verifying causal coupling could be beneficial before treating model-generated explanations as evidence about the model's true decision-making process.

Title: Auditing Meta-Cognitive Hallucinations in Reasoning Large Language Models
Snippet: The development of Reasoning Large Language Models (RLLMs) has significantly improved multi-step reasoning capabilities, but it has also made hallucination problems more frequent and harder to eliminate. While existing approaches mitigate hallucinations through external knowledge integration, model parameter analysis, or self-verification, they often fail to capture how hallucinations emerge and evolve across the reasoning chain. In this work, we study the causality of hallucinations under constrained knowledge domains by auditing the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectory and assessing the model's cognitive confidence in potentially erroneous or biased claims. Our analysis reveals that in long-CoT settings, RLLMs can iteratively reinforce biases and errors through flawed reflective reasoning, eventually leading to hallucinated reasoning paths. Surprisingly, even direct interventions at the origin of hallucinations often fail to reverse their effects, as reasoning chains exhibit'chain disloyalty'-- a resistance to correction and a tendency to preserve flawed logic. Furthermore, we show that existing hallucination detection methods are less reliable and interpretable than previously assumed in complex reasoning scenarios. Unlike methods such as circuit tracing that require access to model internals, our black-box auditing approach supports interpretable long-chain hallucination attribution, offering better generalizability and practical utility. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Winnie-Lian/AHa_Meta_Cognitive

Title: Loki's Dance of Illusions: A Comprehensive Survey of Hallucination in Large Language Models
Snippet: In this section, we have elaborated on the critical concepts of hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs), including their formal definitions, primary categorizations-factual, faithfulness, and logical fallacy hallucinations-as well as how these hallucinations arise and evolve through the model's training processes of pre-training and post-training. We also explored the significance of confidence calibration in LLMs and how training phases impact this aspect. This sets a solid groundwork for a deeper understanding and the addressing of hallucination issues. We begin by addressing the issue of hallucinations within large language models.

Title: A Novel Differential Feature Learning for Effective Hallucination Detection and Classification
Snippet: Large language models frequently generate hallucinations that pose significant challenges for real-world deployment. In healthcare applications, hallucinated medical information could impact patient care decisions, while in legal contexts, factually incorrect analysis could affect case outcomes. Financial systems face risks from erroneous market analysis leading to poor investment decisions. These high-stakes applications have driven extensive research into hallucination detection methods, with approaches evolving from simple confidencebased measures to sophisticated internal representation analysis. 

Early detection efforts focused on output-level validation methods. Uncertainty estimation approaches measure model confidence through entropy and predictive variance [5], [6], while masked language model techniques analyze probability distributions to identify inconsistencies [7]. Self-consistency methods generate multiple responses to the same query and identify variations as potential hallucinations [8]. Contrastive learning approaches train models to distinguish between factual and hallucinated content through explicit negative sampling [10]. Evidence retrieval methods decompose generated text into atomic facts and verify them against external knowledge sources [15], while cross-model validation employs one  language model to audit another's outputs through systematic examination [16]. However, these approaches face inherent limitations: uncertainty methods fail when models express high confidence in incorrect content [7], self-consistency cannot distinguish consistently erroneous information [8], and evidence retrieval encounters scalability challenges [15], [16]. 

Motivated by these limitations, recent research has shifted toward internal representation analysis as an alternative paradigm. Studies have shown that specific hidden layers exhibit distributional differences between hallucinatory and factual content [11]. Building upon the Transformer architecture [17], differential attention mechanisms have demonstrated efficacy in amplifying task-relevant information while attenuating noise [13]. However, current layer-level approaches process entire hidden representations uniformly, typically extracting complete 768-dimensional vectors without examining internal feature importance. 

While layer-level analysis has advanced understanding of hallucination mechanisms, it overlooks the internal structure of hidden representations. Few studies have systematically examined which specific feature dimensions within layers carry hallucination-relevant information. This leaves open questions about whether detection systems could operate more efficiently by focusing on discriminative feature subsets rather than processing entire representations.

documents.title: Auditing Meta-Cognitive Hallucinations in Reasoning Large Language Models
documents.snippet: The development of Reasoning Large Language Models (RLLMs) has significantly improved multi-step reasoning capabilities, but it has also made hallucination problems more frequent and harder to eliminate. While existing approaches mitigate hallucinations through external knowledge integration, model parameter analysis, or self-verification, they often fail to capture how hallucinations emerge and evolve across the reasoning chain. In this work, we study the causality of hallucinations under constrained knowledge domains by auditing the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectory and assessing the model's cognitive confidence in potentially erroneous or biased claims. Our analysis reveals that in long-CoT settings, RLLMs can iteratively reinforce biases and errors through flawed reflective reasoning, eventually leading to hallucinated reasoning paths. Surprisingly, even direct interventions at the origin of hallucinations often fail to reverse their effects, as reasoning chains exhibit'chain disloyalty'-- a resistance to correction and a tendency to preserve flawed logic. Furthermore, we show that existing hallucination detection methods are less reliable and interpretable than previously assumed in complex reasoning scenarios. Unlike methods such as circuit tracing that require access to model internals, our black-box auditing approach supports interpretable long-chain hallucination attribution, offering better generalizability and practical utility. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Winnie-Lian/AHa_Meta_Cognitive

This sets a solid groundwork for a deeper understanding and the addressing of hallucination issues. We begin by addressing the issue of hallucinations within large language models.

documents.title: A Novel Differential Feature Learning for Effective Hallucination Detection and Classification
documents.snippet:
Large language models frequently generate hallucinations that pose significant challenges for real-world deployment. In healthcare applications, hallucinated medical information could impact patient care decisions, while in legal contexts, factually incorrect analysis could affect case outcomes. Financial systems face risks from erroneous market analysis leading to poor investment decisions. These high-stakes applications have driven extensive research into hallucination detection methods, with approaches evolving from simple confidencebased measures to sophisticated internal representation analysis. 

Early detection efforts focused on output-level validation methods. Uncertainty estimation approaches measure model confidence through entropy and predictive variance [5], [6], while masked language model techniques analyze probability distributions to identify inconsistencies [7]. Self-consistency methods generate multiple responses to the same query and identify variations as potential hallucinations [8]. Contrastive learning approaches train models to distinguish between factual and hallucinated content through explicit negative sampling [10]. Evidence retrieval methods decompose generated text into atomic facts and verify them against external knowledge sources [15], while cross-model validation employs one  language model to audit another's outputs through systematic examination [16]. However, these approaches face inherent limitations: uncertainty methods fail when models express high confidence in incorrect content [7], self-consistency cannot distinguish consistently erroneous information [8], and evidence retrieval encounters scalability challenges [15], [16]. 

Motivated by these limitations, recent research has shifted toward internal representation analysis as an alternative paradigm. Studies have shown that specific hidden layers exhibit distributional differences between hallucinatory and factual content [11]. Building upon the Transformer architecture [17], differential attention mechanisms have demonstrated efficacy in amplifying task-relevant information while attenuating noise [13]. However, current layer-level approaches process entire hidden representations uniformly, typically extracting complete 768-dimensional vectors without examining internal feature importance. 

While layer-level analysis has advanced understanding of hallucination mechanisms, it overlooks the internal structure of hidden representations. Few studies have systematically examined which specific feature dimensions within layers carry hallucination-relevant information. This leaves open questions about whether detection systems could operate more efficiently by focusing on discriminative feature subsets rather than processing entire representations.

The claim “no method yet provides comprehensive understanding of model decision-making” can be evaluated by asking whether current mechanistic interpretability (MI) methods (a) recover faithful, general, and human-understandable mechanisms across capabilities, and (b) withstand scrutiny, transfer across architectures/scales/domains, and enable robust steering. Recent work shows striking progress in narrow domains—e.g., arithmetic, logic, and internal planning—using circuits, sparse autoencoders/transcoders, and causal interventions. <cite id="74772c97-0">Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer transformer computations into human-understandable parts and has explained key phenomena such as in-context learning via a characteristic two-head circuit, polysemantic neurons replaced by sparser, more interpretable features via SAEs, and multi-step reasoning audited with cross-layer transcoders, though methods are still developing</cite>. At the same time, surveys and critical evaluations argue that core desiderata—faithfulness, generality, selectivity, and human understandability—are only partially satisfied, and faithfulness itself is approximate and distribution-relative. <cite id="62936aa8-0">State-of-the-art MI defines faithfulness, sparsity/minimality, generality (evaluated on out-of-distribution data), selectivity, and human understandability as key metrics, notes that generality is rare and hard to measure, and highlights the difficulty of reliably quantifying human understandability</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-3">Explanatory faithfulness should match internal steps to mechanisms for generalization, not just behavioral correlation, yet explanation quality depends on goals and is non-binary; emergent behavior remains opaque despite knowledge of low-level components</cite>.

Narrow-domain breakthroughs: what is now well-explained
Recent studies demonstrate concrete, validated mechanisms for specific capabilities using circuit decomposition and causal tools. <cite id="74772c97-1">Digit-position-specific arithmetic circuits have been identified and causally verified via targeted interventions, showing that LLMs compute modular arithmetic digit-by-digit; however, debates persist over whether models implement algorithmic rules or ensembles of heuristics, leaving a unified arithmetic account open</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-2">Circuit analyses have been applied to propositional logic, shifting interpretability from benchmarking to fine-grained decomposition of reasoning components and extending prior MI insights from arithmetic, syllogisms, graph connectivity, VLM tasks, and indirect object identification</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-0">In-context learning has been linked to a characteristic two-head circuit emerging during a training phase change, with perturbation support; sparse autoencoders and transcoders recover monosemantic features and separate input-invariant from input-dependent components, enabling auditing of multi-step reasoning with cross-layer analyses</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-3">Transformer circuits formalize models as DAGs of heads/MLPs and emphasize that compact, faithful circuits allow precise and efficient interpretability, tying circuit minimality to explanatory power</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-0">Mathematically grounded perspectives complement empirical tools: automata analyses show attention can implement finite-state algorithms; optimization views connect in-context learning to preconditioned gradient steps; and mean-field theory yields global convergence guarantees at scale</cite>.

These advances falsify “no understanding” in specific niches but reveal scope limits. <cite id="74772c97-1">Even in arithmetic—where multiple studies converge—there is disagreement over whether mechanisms reflect true numerical computation or symbolic pattern recognition, and whether numbers are represented as generalized helices via a “Clock” algorithm</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-1">Probing fails to recover exact numeric values but succeeds at recovering digits, indicating base-10 digit-wise representations, underscoring that representation-level insights can be partial and task-specific</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-2">In logic, prior fine-grained analyses cover limited problem classes and leave open combinations of variable relationships, value assignments, and queries, indicating incomplete coverage</cite>.

Limits: faithfulness that is approximate, fragile, and distribution-relative
Surveys emphasize that faithfulness in MI is inherently a continuum and must be balanced against complexity, with generality and selectivity often under-measured. <cite id="62936aa8-0">Faithfulness is a generalization of causal mediation and commonly measured; sparsity/minimality aids minimality but is not as prevalent; generality requires OOD evaluation and is increasingly recognized as crucial but rare; selectivity is seldom measured; and human understandability remains difficult to quantify reliably</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-2">Circuit-faithfulness is measured via ablated-model fidelity; any interpretation is an approximation that necessarily omits aspects of behavior, and MI seeks faithful, human-understandable explanations via analysis of features and algorithms, with representation engineering as a tool for steering</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-3">Explanatory faithfulness aligns internal activations step-by-step with mechanistic explanations over data distributions, but emergent behavior remains opaque despite low-level knowledge, and faithfulness is relative and approximate</cite>.

Empirical robustness concerns cut both ways. <cite id="62936aa8-2">Transformer circuit faithfulness has been shown not to be robust: ablations that match behavior can fail on other inputs, highlighting the fragility of circuit-level claims</cite>. On the representation/steering side, adversarial and interventionist work shows that behaviors—including safety and reasoning mechanisms—can be destabilized or flipped with bounded latent or parameter-space perturbations. <cite id="db7a62db-1">Mechanistic MI relies on probes, SAEs, activation patching, and interchange interventions; a representation-aware robustness framework uses soft parameter/latent-space interventions to show how safety behavior can be destabilized under bounded perturbations, introducing a latent vulnerability score across layers and alignment strategies</cite>. While this piece centers on safety, it underscores that circuit-level mechanisms can be undermined without global architectural change. Broader adversarial literature and transformer-specific attacks show that attention-based mechanisms and self-attention components are malleable targets. <cite id="db7a62db-0">Adversarial attacks alter attention maps; training-time defenses enforce similar attentions for clean/adversarial inputs; and sparsity has been leveraged to improve robustness (often with retraining), revealing the tight coupling between interpretability signals and vulnerability</cite>. <cite id="db7a62db-4">White-box attacks like Patch-Fool and Attention-Fool directly perturb patches or attention scores to fool ViTs; black-box extensions refine transferability via token gradients and selective patch removal, showing that attention-centric MI signals can be targeted</cite>. <cite id="db7a62db-3">Patch-Fool demonstrates that ViTs’ robustness can be overturned under dedicated attacks by manipulating self-attention at the patch level, indicating that perceived robustness can be brittle</cite>. Together, these results suggest that even well-validated mechanisms can be adversarially nullified or repurposed, so “faithful today, fragile tomorrow” remains a practical risk.

Breadth across domains and tasks: uneven progress and open gaps
Surveys and overviews argue MI methods are advancing but remain narrow in scope and immature. <cite id="74772c97-0">Frontier-scale case studies use cross-layer transcoders to trace multi-step reasoning and other behaviors, illustrating auditing tools, but overall note that MI methods are still developing</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-1">Compositional interpretability frames actionable interpretability via symmetries and MDL, connecting to top-down hypothesis testing and bottom-up model design; yet applying such constraints to black-box mechanistic or post-hoc interpretations is difficult, highlighting structural gaps in scalable, general methods</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-0">Recent work stresses that generality requires OOD evaluation and that human understandability is not yet reliably measurable, reinforcing that current mechanisms often fail to transfer</cite>.

Within NLP, progress is patchy and contested. <cite id="74772c97-1">Arithmetic studies report digit-wise mechanisms with causal support, but other work argues LLMs rely on a bag of heuristics rather than a single algorithm, and probes recover digits but not exact numbers, evidencing both insight and incompleteness</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-2">Circuit analyses in logic extend prior work across several subdomains, yet they explicitly target narrow problem classes and do not cover the full space of variable relations, values, and queries</cite>. Beyond language, MI-style tools are being explored in vision and multimodal settings, but robust, cross-task mechanistic accounts remain limited. <cite id="db7a62db-4">Transformer adversarial attacks (Patch-Fool, Attention-Fool, PAR) target attention mechanisms directly, and transferable black-box methods exploit token-level gradients and query-based removals, indicating that core representational mechanisms in vision transformers are malleable</cite>. <cite id="db7a62db-1">Latent-space interventions demonstrate that safety behaviors can be destabilized under bounded perturbations across layers and alignment strategies, suggesting that high-level behaviors are sensitive to internal changes not captured by local circuit stories</cite>.

Synthesis: Does “no comprehensive understanding” still hold?
Given narrow-domain circuit successes, the strongest version of the claim—that “no method yet provides any understanding at all”—is clearly too strong. <cite id="74772c97-0">Transformer internals have been decomposed into human-understandable components and circuits, with causal evidence for in-context learning mechanisms, polysemantic-to-monosemantic feature transforms, and cross-layer reasoning pathways</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-1">Digit-wise arithmetic circuits and logic circuits show that specific algorithmic capabilities can be identified and causally validated in parts of the hypothesis space</cite>. However, the qualified claim—that “no method yet provides comprehensive, robust, cross-capability, and human-understandable explanations that withstand adversarial or architectural change”—is well supported. <cite id="62936aa8-0">Surveys emphasize that faithfulness, generality, selectivity, and human understandability are only partially achieved; generality requires OOD evaluation and is rarely measured, and human understandability is hard to quantify</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-2">Circuit faithfulness is not robust and must be viewed as a continuum of approximation</cite>. <cite id="db7a62db-1">Representation-level interventions can destabilize safety behaviors under bounded perturbations, implying that high-level mechanisms are fragile</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-1">Even within arithmetic, researchers disagree on whether models implement algorithms or heuristic ensembles, and probing reveals digit-wise representations rather than full numeric quantities</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-2">Logic circuit work covers limited problem families and leaves open compositionality across constructs</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-0">Mathematically grounded analyses (finite-state algorithms, gradient interpretations, mean-field convergence) illuminate parts of the computation but do not constitute a unified, mechanistic theory across all capabilities</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-3">Explanatory faithfulness aims at mechanism-level alignment, yet emergent behavior remains opaque and faithfulness is relative and approximate</cite>.

What would invalidate the claim?
Two evidence patterns would substantially weaken the claim. First, a cross-capability, architecture-agnostic explanatory theory whose mechanisms (i) match internal activations step-by-step across diverse tasks (math, logic, planning, VLMs, code), (ii) exhibit robustness to adversarial/latent perturbations, and (iii) enable reliable steering and safety guarantees via representation engineering. <cite id="62936aa8-0">Achieving measurable generality and human understandability across OOD data and tasks would directly address major gaps</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-2">Demonstrating robustness of circuit-faithfulness beyond local neighborhoods would resolve fragility concerns</cite>. <cite id="db7a62db-1">Proving latent vulnerability bounds that resist bounded interventions across alignment strategies would show mechanism-level stability</cite>. Second, broad unification showing that narrow circuits compose into a coherent computational semantics—e.g., arithmetic and logic mechanisms integrate into a general-purpose algorithmic substrate that generalizes and transfers under distribution shift—rather than remaining task-specific heuristics. <cite id="74772c97-1">Resolving arithmetic’s algorithm-vs-heuristics debate in favor of a unified algorithmic account that transfers would be a landmark advance</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-2">Extending fine-grained reasoning analyses to cover variable-relationship compositionality across tasks would demonstrate breadth</cite>.

Caveats and outlook
Two caveats temper conclusions. First, MI methods are improving rapidly: better sparsity (SAEs, transcoders), stronger causal tools (activation patching, compact faithful circuits), and formal metrics for faithfulness and complexity point toward scalable, principled discovery. <cite id="74772c97-0">Sparse autoencoders and transcoders separate input-invariant and input-dependent components and match/surpass SAEs in sparsity, faithfulness, and interpretability, enabling multi-step reasoning audits</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-1">Compositional and actionable interpretability frameworks propose efficient faithfulness/complexity optimization and connect top-down testing to bottom-up design</cite>. Second, robustness-to-transfer remains the bottleneck. <cite id="62936aa8-2">Faithfulness is inherently approximate and fragile</cite>. <cite id="db7a62db-1">Latent-space interventions destabilize safety behaviors under bounded changes</cite>. <cite id="db7a62db-4">Attention-centric attacks show that core representational mechanisms can be flipped</cite>. Until mechanisms exhibit distributional and adversarial stability with cross-domain generality, the cautious claim—that comprehensive, reliable mechanistic understanding remains out of reach—remains well supported.

Bottom line
Narrow-domain breakthroughs have definitively invalidated the idea that “no understanding” is possible at all: specific capabilities now have validated, causal mechanistic accounts. <cite id="74772c97-0">Internal planning, in-context learning circuits, and cross-layer reasoning decompositions show that human-understandable mechanisms operate within transformers</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-1,74772c97-2">Arithmetic and logic circuits demonstrate algorithmic-like behavior with causal interventions, though unified accounts and full coverage remain open</cite>. However, the broader claim—that we lack comprehensive, robust, and general methods for understanding decision-making across capabilities and architectures—also stands: faithfulness is approximate and fragile, generality/selectivity/understandability are under-measured, and adversarial/latent perturbations can nullify mechanisms. <cite id="62936aa8-0">Surveys emphasize the need for robust generality and reliable human understandability</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-2">Circuit faithfulness is not robust</cite>. <cite id="db7a62db-1">Safety behaviors are dissociable under bounded latent perturbations</cite>. Therefore, the most accurate assessment is qualified: narrow-domain mechanistic advances have not invalidated the overarching claim; rather, they coexist with persistent limits, so comprehensive, cross-capability understanding remains an open goal. <cite id="74772c97-0">Frontier-scale case studies show progress and tool readiness, yet methods are still developing</cite>. <cite id="74772c97-1">Open debates and partial representation findings within arithmetic/logic underscore incomplete explanations</cite>. <cite id="62936aa8-3">Emergent behavior’s opacity and the non-binary nature of faithfulness caution against over-claiming comprehensive mechanisms</cite>.
